display_name: Shafer Vineyards One Point Five, Napa Valley
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The name refers to the 1.5 miles between the Stags Leap District vineyard and the winery cave, signaling a wine built on estate heritage despite the broader Napa Valley designation. This bottling delivers the plush ripeness expected from the region's warm pockets without the single-vineyard price tag of Hillside Select.",
  "wine_summary": "Shafer Vineyards established itself during the 1970s when Napa was still proving its longevity, focusing on deep color and concentration. One Point Five acts as the entry point to their portfolio, blending estate fruit from the Stags Leap District with selected lots from across the valley floor. The result prioritizes immediate drinkability over the austere structure found in cooler sub-appellations like Rutherford or Oakville.",
  "terroir_expression": "While the broader Napa Valley designation allows blending, the Stags Leap District estate fruit provides the backbone with volcanic soils contributing iron-rich density. Alluvial clay from the valley floor adds mid-palate weight, balancing the firm tannic grip of the hillside plots. The Mediterranean climate here ensures full phenolic ripeness, pushing alcohol to 15.3% and softening the pyrazines that often create green bell pepper notes in cooler sites.",
  "vinification_summary": "Aging in French oak barrels for roughly 18 months follows fermentation in stainless steel tanks. The winemaking team utilizes malolactic conversion, a secondary fermentation where bacteria convert sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, rounding out the mouthfeel. This process, combined with new oak usage, creates the vanilla and cedar notes that frame the black fruit core.",
  "food_pairing": "Serve this alongside smoked brisket with a spicy bark because the fat cuts through the high alcohol and tannins. Bone-in ribeye with charred edges works well since protein softens the grip of the tannins. Nashville hot chicken offers a contrast where the sweetness in the fruit balances the heat. Mushroom risotto with truffle oil mirrors the volcanic soil influence. Lamb shank braised in red wine matches the intensity and savory finish.",
  "comparable_wines": "Caymus Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon — shares the plush, high-alcohol Napa style but lacks the volcanic structure. Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cask 23 — similar Stags Leap District heritage with slightly more restraint. Joseph Phelps Insignia — another Napa Valley blend that prioritizes ripeness and oak integration.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins and ripe dark fruit",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Dark rooms at 55°F preserve the fruit freshness over five years. Decant for one hour before serving to allow the alcohol to integrate.",
  "value_assessment": "$140 places this directly against premium estate bottlings from Oakville and Rutherford. You pay a premium for the Shafer label consistency, which holds value better than many contemporaries on the secondary market. It costs more than Caymus but offers better structural integrity for aging.",
  "market_position": "Throughout the country, sommeliers feature it on lists where guests want a recognized name without navigating obscure producers. The allocation model keeps it off standard retail shelves, requiring a mailing list relationship for consistent access. Collectors target this wine for cellar building because it bridges the gap between entry-level Napa and ultra-premium single vineyards.",
  "insider_take": "Buyers seeking lower alcohol wines with distinct herbal notes should look elsewhere, as the ripeness here dominates the profile. The tradeoff for immediate plushness is less geological specificity than a single-vineyard Stags Leap District bottling. Buy it when you need a crowd-pleaser that signals quality without requiring decades of patience.",
  "aging_potential_years": 15,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 2,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 10,
  "sensory": {

    "body": 5,
    "sweetness": 1,
    "alcohol": 5,
    "color_intensity": "deep",
    "aroma_intensity": "pronounced",
    "finish_length": "long",
    "complexity": "complex",
    "quality_level": "outstanding"
  }
}

parsed.hook: The name refers to the 1.5 miles between the Stags Leap District vineyard and the winery cave, signaling a wine built on estate heritage despite the broader Napa Valley designation. This bottling delivers the plush ripeness expected from the region's warm pockets without the single-vineyard price tag of Hillside Select.
parsed.wine_summary: Shafer Vineyards established itself during the 1970s when Napa was still proving its longevity, focusing on deep color and concentration. One Point Five acts as the entry point to their portfolio, blending estate fruit from the Stags Leap District with selected lots from across the valley floor. The result prioritizes immediate drinkability over the austere structure found in cooler sub-appellations like Rutherford or Oakville.
parsed.terroir_expression: While the broader Napa Valley designation allows blending, the Stags Leap District estate fruit provides the backbone with volcanic soils contributing iron-rich density. Alluvial clay from the valley floor adds mid-palate weight, balancing the firm tannic grip of the hillside plots. The Mediterranean climate here ensures full phenolic ripeness, pushing alcohol to 15.3% and softening the pyrazines that often create green bell pepper notes in cooler sites.
parsed.vinification_summary: Aging in French oak barrels for roughly 18 months follows fermentation in stainless steel tanks. The winemaking team utilizes malolactic conversion, a secondary fermentation where bacteria convert sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, rounding out the mouthfeel. This process, combined with new oak usage, creates the vanilla and cedar notes that frame the black fruit core.
parsed.food_pairing: Serve this alongside smoked brisket with a spicy bark because the fat cuts through the high alcohol and tannins. Bone-in ribeye with charred edges works well since protein softens the grip of the tannins. Nashville hot chicken offers a contrast where the sweetness in the fruit balances the heat. Mushroom risotto with truffle oil mirrors the volcanic soil influence. Lamb shank braised in red wine matches the intensity and savory finish.
parsed.comparable_wines: Caymus Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon — shares the plush, high-alcohol Napa style but lacks the volcanic structure. Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cask 23 — similar Stags Leap District heritage with slightly more restraint. Joseph Phelps Insignia — another Napa Valley blend that prioritizes ripeness and oak integration.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins and ripe dark fruit
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Dark rooms at 55°F preserve the fruit freshness over five years. Decant for one hour before serving to allow the alcohol to integrate.
parsed.value_assessment: $140 places this directly against premium estate bottlings from Oakville and Rutherford. You pay a premium for the Shafer label consistency, which holds value better than many contemporaries on the secondary market. It costs more than Caymus but offers better structural integrity for aging.
parsed.market_position: Throughout the country, sommeliers feature it on lists where guests want a recognized name without navigating obscure producers. The allocation model keeps it off standard retail shelves, requiring a mailing list relationship for consistent access. Collectors target this wine for cellar building because it bridges the gap between entry-level Napa and ultra-premium single vineyards.
parsed.insider_take: Buyers seeking lower alcohol wines with distinct herbal notes should look elsewhere, as the ripeness here dominates the profile. The tradeoff for immediate plushness is less geological specificity than a single-vineyard Stags Leap District bottling. Buy it when you need a crowd-pleaser that signals quality without requiring decades of patience.
